rv.q: ...it’s a slight disappointment when the play’s denouement tips into overexplanation.
Practically humming with tension, Bonds’s many-layered play moves through time, shuffling realities, tracing Ana’s trauma, disorienting us.

While on the level of character depiction “Jonah” holds our attention, its episodic nature, stretches of mundane dialogue and the disjointed narrative lead to a certain frustration: Where we are in Ana’s life is impossible to pin down, and the jumpy story is more confusing than illuminating.
The fledgling lovers’ interactions come across as thoroughly believable and – since we’ve all been there at one point in our lives – unbelievably touching.
With its easygoing wit, appealing characters, and underlying vein of deep feeling, I suspect it will be taken up by theatres around the country.
You’ll do that anyway, since director Danya Taymor’s fine-tuned cast will keep you glued.
Rachel Bonds’ fascinating new play finds hope in an author’s imagination
Beans registers each emotion with complete authenticity (even if Ana’s truthfulness is in question) and makes Ana one of the most interesting protagonists currently on the New York stage.
Fine acting, with Beans as its strong core, make Jonah a worthy look at the stories we tell ourselves.
It’s too bad that the performances sometimes get lost in a play that seems cleverer than it is.

It was at comic moments like these that I felt sorry that “Jonah” wasn’t the light romantic comedy that it initially promised to be – followed by guilt that I didn’t more fully appreciate the more sophisticated, if more challenging, drama it turned out to be.
Jonah, which will likely get multiple regional performances, holds the attention, but it’s simply too gimmicky and cerebrally challenging for complete emotional appreciation.

While Rachel Bonds’ Jonah seems very thin aside from its tricky chronology and hidden secrets, it is an interesting portrait of disaffected youth told through the story of one young indomitable woman.

The flashy production emphasizes the work’s concerns with technique and presumed importance over simple storytelling. The final scenes are affective, but the play is ultimately more of an exercise rather than a satisfying theatrical experience; it does succeed as a showcase for its gifted cast.

It's the cleverest of constructs, looking at trauma and pain from a number of angles and vantage points, all at once, from up above, back and forward, and within such a detailed and unique lyrical unwrapping.
Jonah is a well-structured puzzle-box of a play, a portrait of the artist as a young woman — and a preternatural survivor.

Jonah was a beautifully crafted play with just the right amount of ambiguity to keep the audience intrigued about what we were seeing but also enjoying puzzling out the possible relationships between the scenes.
With good performances and excellent writing, “Jonah” provides viewers with some meaty ideas to discuss-including the nature of Jonah himself.
Kudos to the four actors whose performances make this transition from fantasy to redemptive reality authentic and believable.
It’s an empathetic, piercing drama, yet its storytelling machinations give it an air of complexity that Ana’s fairly commonplace experiences don’t necessarily merit.
The intentional elusiveness of such an unreliable narrator can become unintentionally alienating.
Whether you believe in a supreme being or not, you’ll come away from Jonah believing in Ana, and in Beans.

cn.t: Critics find Rachel Bonds' non-linear drama intriguing but elusive, praising Gabby Beans' magnetic performance while noting the play's deliberately slippery structure leaves many audiences puzzled about what they've witnessed.
